articles.title: The Man Who Went Into Labor Twice
articles.dek: Paul reaches for the rawest image he can find to describe a love that won't let you stay half-grown — and it changes what "born again" was always meant to mean.
articles.quote: The second labor wasn't proof the first one had failed. It was proof that someone refused to let what had been started stay unfinished.
articles.body:
In August 2024, at Bercy Arena in Paris, Simone Biles walked up to the balance beam for an Olympic final, and half the crowd was holding its breath before she even mounted it. Three years earlier, at the Tokyo Olympics, she had stepped off a vault mid-air, disoriented, unable to tell up from down. Gymnasts call it "the twisties." Her brain and her body, which had worked as one thing for twenty years, had suddenly come unglued from each other. She withdrew from the competition and flew home while the whole world watched and argued about what it meant.

She did not quit. She went back to the same gym, the same coaches, and started over with the basics: handstands, cartwheels, the shapes she had first learned as a six-year-old. Not because she had forgotten how to do a giant swing or a double layout. She already knew. The knowledge was in her. What had broken was the connection between what she knew and what her body would actually do. So for two years she rebuilt that connection, piece by piece, until in Paris she stood on the beam and her body did, without hesitation, everything she had already once been able to do. Gold. Tears. Her teammates lifting her off the mat. Everyone said "she's back." But it was not quite that. She had been re-formed.

There is a strange line in Paul's letter to the Galatians that only makes full sense next to a story like that. Paul is writing to churches he himself brought to faith. He reminds them, earlier in the letter, of what they already have: "before the coming of this faith, we were held in custody under the law," he writes, "locked up until the faith that was to come would be revealed" (Galatians 3:23). Then Christ came, and everything changed. "So in Christ Jesus you are all children of God through faith... There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:26, 28). In chapter four he pushes the picture further: an heir who is still a child is no different from a slave, kept under guardians and trustees until the time set by his father. But "when the set time had fully come, God sent his Son... to redeem those under the law, that we might receive adoption to sonship" (Galatians 4:4-5). Not servants anymore. Sons and daughters, crying out "Abba, Father," and heirs of everything.

That should have settled the matter for good. But new teachers had arrived in Galatia insisting that faith in Christ was not quite enough — that these believers also needed circumcision, needed to keep the old calendar of days and months and seasons, needed to go back under the very guardians Christ had freed them from. And Paul, watching people he loves start climbing back into a cage they had already walked out of, writes one of the rawest sentences in the New Testament.

"My dear children, for whom I am again in the pains of childbirth until Christ is formed in you, how I wish I could be with you now and change my tone, because I am perplexed about you!" (Galatians 4:19-20)

Notice the word "again." Paul had already given birth to this church once — he was the one who first preached Christ to them, and they had received him "as if I were an angel of God" (Galatians 4:14). They were not unborn. They were his children, already. And yet here he is, a grown man, reaching for the most physical, most costly image available to him — labor pains — to describe what it now takes to keep them. It is worth asking why he doesn't just say "I'm disappointed" or "please reconsider." He says he is in labor. Twice, for the same children.

There is also a word tucked into that verse easy to read past: "formed." In the original language it's the term used for an embryo taking shape inside the womb — not decoration added to the outside, but a form developing from within. Paul isn't laboring to add one more belief to their list. He's laboring for Christ's actual shape to emerge in them, the way a child's features slowly take form before anyone can see them. That is close to what happened to Biles. Her comeback wasn't learning something new. It was recovering, piece by piece, a form she already had inside her but had lost the use of. The second labor wasn't proof the first one had failed. It was proof that someone refused to let what had been started stay unfinished.

That is worth sitting with if you have ever felt like your faith is starting over from zero. Maybe you once knew, all the way to your bones, that you were loved and forgiven and free — and somewhere along the way you slid back into counting your good deeds, measuring your standing with God by how well you performed that week, keeping score the way the Galatians had gone back to keeping the calendar. Paul doesn't shame anyone in that church for the slide. He labors for them. He would rather go through the pain of birthing them again than let them stay half-formed.

So ask yourself two questions today. First: who has been in labor for you — a mother who kept praying long after you stopped listening, a mentor who kept showing up after you'd disappointed them once, a friend who refuses to give up on who you're becoming? Thank that person, if you can, before the week is out. Second: is there someone God is asking you to labor for — not to fix, not to lecture, but to stay with, in prayer and patience, until Christ takes shape in them too?

Simone Biles didn't need anyone to tell her she used to be great. She needed people willing to stay in the gym with her while her body slowly remembered what it already knew. That is the kind of love Paul is describing. Not a love that gives up when you regress, but one willing to labor again, for as long as it takes, until you are fully formed.

articles.title: The Letter Hezekiah Spread Out
articles.dek: When Jerusalem's enemy sent a written threat designed to break him, the king did something with the paper itself that changed everything.
articles.quote: What gets honestly opened in God's presence rarely finishes the fight it started.
articles.body:
In the early 1980s, a psychologist named James Pennebaker ran an experiment that puzzled his own research team. He asked a group of college students to write, for fifteen minutes a day, four days in a row, about the most traumatic experience of their lives — the thing they had never fully told anyone. A second group wrote about something trivial, like their dorm room furniture. Nothing else changed. Same students, same semester, same stress of exams and homesickness.

Six months later, the difference showed up in their blood. The students who had written honestly about their pain had stronger immune function, measurably more active natural killer cells, and made far fewer visits to the campus health center than the students who wrote about furniture. Pennebaker hadn't given anyone therapy. He had simply given them a place to lay the thing out in full view, in their own handwriting, instead of carrying it folded up and hidden inside. The body, it turns out, keeps a different kind of score when a wound stays sealed than when it is opened and looked at honestly.

Centuries before any of that could be measured, a king in Jerusalem discovered something almost identical — not about trauma, but about terror.

By the time we reach Isaiah 37, Judah is finished, or so it looks. The Assyrian army, the most feared war machine of the ancient world, has already swallowed the northern kingdom of Israel and dozens of fortified cities. Now King Sennacherib's field commander stands outside Jerusalem's walls, shouting in Hebrew loud enough for the people on the ramparts to hear, mocking their God by name, daring them to believe he can save them. It is psychological warfare, and it works. King Hezekiah tears his clothes in grief and puts on sackcloth — the ancient posture of a man out of options.

Then Sennacherib does something almost cruel in its precision. He doesn't just threaten Jerusalem again. He sends Hezekiah a letter — an actual written document, carried by messengers, restating the taunt in ink so it can be read, reread, and left to fester in a drawer. Letters do that. They don't fade with the sound of a shouting voice; they sit, waiting to be reopened at two in the morning.

Here is where the story turns, and it turns on something almost nobody notices the first time through. Hezekiah does not burn the letter. He does not stuff it away and pretend composure. He does not even pray about it from a safe distance. He takes the letter, walks up to the temple, and does this:

Hezekiah received the letter from the messengers and read it. Then he went up to the temple of the LORD and spread it out before the LORD. (Isaiah 37:14, NIV)

Spread it out. Not crumpled it in a fist and shook it at heaven. Not summarized the gist in a whispered prayer. He unfolded the actual document — every insult, every threat, every word designed to make him feel small and alone — flat, in full, in the one place built to hold what he could not carry by himself.

It's worth asking why this detail made it into Scripture at all. The writer could have simply said, "Hezekiah prayed." Instead we get the physical mechanics of it: receive, read, go up, spread out. It reads almost like stage directions, because it is one. This is a king refusing to manage his fear privately. He is bringing the whole, unedited threat into the light, in front of the only witness who could actually do something about it.

And what follows is not a tidy resolution manufactured by human effort. Isaiah sends word that God has heard, and that very night — the text tells us — an angel of the Lord went out and struck down the Assyrian camp, and Sennacherib withdrew and was later killed by his own sons while worshiping in his own temple (Isaiah 37:36-38). The threat that had been spread out on temple stone came to nothing. But notice the order of events. Deliverance came after the letter was opened before God, not before.

This is where the parallel with Pennebaker's students becomes useful — not because prayer is a coping technique, but because both point at the same quiet truth about how fear actually behaves: it grows in the dark and loses ground in the light. What Hezekiah refused to do was manage the threat alone, in his own head, behind a closed door. He brought the specific words — not a vague, generalized worry, but the actual document — into a relationship. That is the difference between anxiety and prayer. Anxiety rehearses the threat in isolation. Prayer spreads it out in front of someone.

Most of us are holding a letter right now. Maybe it's an actual one — a diagnosis on paper, a termination notice, a message from someone who wants to hurt you. Maybe it isn't paper at all, just words that keep replaying: a doctor's phrase, a boss's tone, a phone call you're dreading. The instinct is the same one Hezekiah could have followed and didn't: fold it small, tuck it away, manage it quietly, tell no one, especially not God, as if bringing it into prayer would somehow make it more real than it already is.

But the text suggests the opposite is true. The letter was already real. Jerusalem was already surrounded. What changed wasn't the danger — it was where the danger got laid out, and in whose presence. Hezekiah's prayer in the following verses is worth reading slowly (Isaiah 37:16-20); he doesn't ask God to simply make him feel better. He asks God to look, to listen, to see, using the very letter as evidence: "turn your ear, LORD, and listen; open your eyes, LORD, and see" (Isaiah 37:17). He points at the specific words on the page. He doesn't pray in generalities. Neither should we.

So here is something practical to keep this week, small enough to actually do: the next time a fear starts running laps in your head at night, don't just think about it — say it out loud, or write it down, specifically, and bring that exact thing to God in prayer. Not "help me with everything," but the actual sentence someone said, the actual number on the test result, the actual fear by name. Spread it out. You are not informing God of anything he doesn't already know. You are doing what Hezekiah did — refusing to carry alone what was never meant to be carried alone.

The Assyrian letter is long gone, dust for twenty-seven centuries. But the pattern it revealed hasn't aged a day: what gets honestly opened in God's presence rarely finishes the fight it started.

articles.title: The Library That Never Burns
articles.dek: In West Africa, a family's entire history can live inside one person's memory — and Psalm 105 asks God's people to guard an even greater story the very same way, one voice at a time.
articles.quote: Memory that stays silent dies with you. Memory that is spoken becomes an inheritance.
articles.body:
In the villages of Mali, in West Africa, there are men and women called griots — jeliw, in the Mandinka tongue — whose entire life's work is memory. From childhood they are apprenticed, sometimes for twenty years, to an elder griot who teaches them to hold in their minds the names, marriages, wars, and songs of families going back centuries. They learn to play the kora, a twenty-one-string harp carved from a gourd, and they learn something harder: thousands of names, in order, ready the moment they're needed. When a wedding happens, or a child is named, or a chief is installed, the griot stands and sings the family's whole history aloud, grandfather by grandfather, deed by deed, without a single page of notes.

The Malian writer Amadou Hampâté Bâ explained why this mattered so much to his people: "In Africa, when an old man dies, a library burns to the ground." A griot is that library, kept alive by breath instead of paper, by voice instead of shelves.

The kora player Toumani Diabaté, one of Mali's most celebrated musicians, comes from a line of griots his own family traces back more than seventy generations — an unbroken chain of fathers teaching sons to remember, so a nation's story would never depend on one fragile scroll, or one surviving elder. Ask a griot why they carry so much, and the answer is always some version of the same thing: someone has to. If no one speaks it, it disappears.

Filipinos know a smaller, gentler version of this. It's the lola on the porch retelling, for the hundredth time, how Lolo courted her during the war. It's the tita who always tells the same story at every reunion, and everyone lets her, because if she stops telling it, who else will? We are, most of us, part griot without ever learning the word for it.

Psalm 105 opens with God asking his people to become griots for him.

The psalm was written to be sung, literally. According to 1 Chronicles 16, when King David finally brought the ark of the covenant into Jerusalem after it had sat forgotten in a farmer's field for twenty years, he didn't just offer a sacrifice and move on. He appointed a man named Asaph and his relatives to stand before the ark and sing, and this song — the very words that open Psalm 105 — was the first thing they sang. Not a private prayer whispered alone. A public performance, meant to be heard by a whole nation, meant to be carried forward by every family that heard it.

Listen to how it opens: "Give praise to the LORD, proclaim his name; make known among the nations what he has done. Sing to him, sing praise to him; tell of all his wonderful acts" (Psalm 105:1–2, NIV). Then, before the psalm ever says the word "remember," it says this: "Glory in his holy name; let the hearts of those who seek the LORD rejoice. Look to the LORD and his strength; seek his face always" (Psalm 105:3–4, NIV). A griot doesn't just recite dry facts about a family. He knows them — their honor, their sorrows, their turning points. Notice where "seek his face" sits: right between the singing and the remembering, as if the psalm is quietly insisting that you cannot faithfully tell someone else the story of what God has done until you've first turned your own face toward him long enough to know it's true.

"Remember the wonders he has done, his miracles, and the judgments he pronounced, you his servants, the offspring of Abraham, his chosen ones, the children of Jacob." (Psalm 105:5–6, NIV)

Here's what's easy to miss on a quick read: this isn't addressed to priests or professional singers. It's addressed to a family — "the offspring of Abraham... the children of Jacob." The people responsible for remembering God's wonders were not specialists set apart for the job. They were sons and daughters, farmers and shepherds, the same people who would go home that evening and put their own children to bed. Memory, in this psalm, was never meant to be a private feeling kept warm in someone's chest. It was assigned. It was handed down like a family trade, the way a griot's father hands the kora to his son.

Notice, too, the order of the verbs across these seven verses: give praise, proclaim, make known, sing, tell, seek, remember. Almost every one of them points outward, toward other people, other nations, the next generation still too young to have seen any of it happen. Only "remember" happens quietly inside a person, and even that one is surrounded on both sides by speech. The psalm never lets memory stay silent for long. It insists that what God has done in your life is not meant to end with you.

Maybe that's worth asking honestly: what has God done in your story that you've never actually said out loud? Not posted online, not journaled privately in the dark, but said, plainly, to a real person, the way a griot sings a name into a room full of witnesses. Perhaps it's how a specific prayer got answered on a specific date you still remember. Perhaps it's a season you survived that, by every reasonable measure, should have broken you. Perhaps it's smaller than that: a provision that arrived at the exact right hour, a warning you somehow heeded, a peace that came from nowhere you can explain.

Those stories are not decoration on a life of faith. According to this psalm, they are inheritance. And an inheritance that isn't spoken has a way of quietly disappearing, the same way a family's history disappears the moment the last person who remembers it stops telling it.

This is where Psalm 105 lands closest to home. God did not ask Israel to build a monument and let it do the remembering for them. He asked them to sing. A monument sits still and waits, passively, to be noticed by whoever happens to walk past. A song has to be carried by a living voice, passed mouth to mouth, generation to generation, which means it only survives if someone keeps choosing, again and again, to open their mouth and tell it one more time.

Memory that stays silent dies with you. Memory that is spoken becomes an inheritance.

You don't need twenty years of training to do what Psalm 105 asks of you. You need one dinner table, one grandchild or godchild, one quiet evening after the rice is finished, and one true sentence: "let me tell you what God did for me." Say it out loud this week, to someone who will remember that you said it. That's how a family, and eventually a whole nation, learns to keep singing long after you're the one who first taught them the tune.

articles.title: No One Needs a Lid for This Bucket
articles.dek: Proverbs says envy quietly rots the bones — and Filipinos already have a name for exactly what that looks like.
articles.quote: Envy doesn't cost the one who rises. It costs the one who reaches up to pull them back down.
articles.illustration: Filipino crab mentality vs. shared catch
articles.body:
Ask a vendor selling live alimango, mud crabs, why she never bothers with a lid on the bucket, and she'll laugh and tell you the truth: she doesn't need one. Put twenty crabs in an open bucket and watch. One will start climbing, legs scrabbling for the rim, almost free — and just as it nears the top, the others reach up and drag it back down. Not to eat it. Not out of hunger. Just to keep it from leaving without them. Filipinos have a name for this, borrowed straight from the bucket: crab mentality. It's the joke at office parties and the quiet accusation at family gatherings — the suspicion that when someone starts to rise, the people around them would rather see them pulled back than see them go up alone.

It's a funny story until you notice how often it's true of hearts, not just crabs. And it turns out a king noticed the same pattern three thousand years before anyone coined the phrase. Solomon's proverbs often come in short, unconnected sayings, but Proverbs 14:26–30 reads like a single thought stretched across five verses, each one circling back to the same question: what is actually holding your heart steady? He starts with security — "Whoever fears the LORD has a secure fortress, and for their children it will be a refuge" (14:26) — and calls that fear of the Lord "a fountain of life" (14:27). Then he turns practical: a nation thrives when it has people, not when its leader hoards glory alone (14:28), and a patient person shows understanding while a quick temper only shows folly (14:29). Then, almost as the quiet verdict on everything before it, he lands here.

A heart at peace gives life to the body, but envy rots the bones. — Proverbs 14:30 (NIV)

Notice what Solomon doesn't say. He doesn't say envy is merely unkind, or embarrassing, or bad manners. He says it rots — the same word used elsewhere for wood eaten through by decay, structure collapsing from the inside while the surface still looks fine. Doctors today would recognize the shape of it: the sleeplessness of comparison, the low simmer of resentment, the way bitterness held too long wears down a body that was never built to carry it. But Solomon's real point isn't medical, it's relational. The crab that pulls another one down doesn't gain anything. It's still in the bucket. Envy doesn't cost the one who rises. It costs the one who reaches up to pull them back down.

Here's the fresh thread worth pulling: envy and fortress, in this passage, aren't two separate topics — they're cause and effect. A heart that has already found its refuge in verse 26 has nothing left to protect in verse 30. It's worth asking why envy grows at all. Usually it's because someone's worth feels unsettled, and another person's rise feels like proof they're losing ground. But Solomon opens this whole passage with a heart that has a fortress already — secure, inherited, not earned by comparison. When your standing doesn't depend on staying ahead of the person next to you, their promotion, their engagement, their answered prayer, stops being a threat. It becomes simply good news for someone you love.

That's the gospel underneath the proverb, even before Christ's name is written anywhere in the Old Testament: security isn't something you defend by keeping others down. It's something given, held, refuged. The whole reason the crab bucket works is that every crab believes there's only one way out, and if someone else takes it, there won't be one left. A heart at peace has already stopped believing that lie.

Not every bucket in the Philippines works like the crab bucket, and that's worth remembering too. Along stretches of the Visayan coast, fisherfolk still keep an old custom. When one banca comes back loaded with the day's catch and a neighbor's boat comes back nearly empty, it isn't unusual for the fuller boat to share right there on the sand — before anyone weighs it, before anyone sells a single fish. No lid needed there either. Just a different kind of heart in the bucket: one that isn't guarding its own rise, because it's already at peace, and a heart at peace can afford to be generous.

You can't control the crabs around you, the coworker who resents your raise or the relative who goes quiet at your good news. But you can choose which bucket your own heart lives in today. The next time you feel that small, familiar pull, someone else's promotion, someone else's bigger catch, someone else's easier season, let it be a signal, not a strategy. Bring it to God before you bring it to anyone else. He's the only fortress secure enough that you never have to reach up and pull someone back down to feel safe inside it. Guard that kind of heart, and Solomon promises something worth holding onto: it gives life, actual life, to the whole body.
